ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: Behavioural Sciences studies how thoughts, emotions and actions influence mental health and illness. It equips clinicians to assess, diagnose and manage psychiatric conditions through evidence‑based communication and therapeutic techniques.

sections.p: Behavioural Sciences integrates psychology, sociology and anthropology to understand patient behaviour, aiding psychiatric diagnosis and formulation.
b: Uses DSM‑5/ICD‑11 criteria for mental disorders
Emphasises history, mental status exam and functional assessment

t.b: What is the current mental state? Identifies thought disorder, mood, cognition, insight.
Does the patient meet criteria for a specific disorder? Confirms diagnosis.

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden, functional impairment and risk, using scales such as PHQ‑9, GAD‑7 or PANSS.
b: Mild: symptoms present, minimal functional loss
Moderate: noticeable impairment, may need medication
Severe: marked dysfunction, high risk of harm

sections.p: Behavioural disturbances arise from biopsychosocial factors; in low‑resource settings infectious and systemic illnesses are common contributors.
b: Psychosocial stressors (trauma, loss, poverty)
Neurochemical imbalance (serotonin, dopamine)
Infections: HIV, TB, malaria affecting CNS
Substance use: alcohol, khat, cannabis
Medical illnesses: hepatitis B, sickle cell, schistosomiasis

sections.p: Patients may report mood changes, anxiety, abnormal thoughts or behaviours, often with impaired daily functioning.
b: Depressed mood, anhedonia, sleep disturbance
Excessive worry, panic attacks, avoidance
Hallucinations, delusions, disorganized speech
Risky or self‑harm behaviours

sections.p: Investigations rule out medical mimics and guide treatment.

t.b: Is there anemia or infection? Anemia may mimic fatigue; infection may cause delirium.
Is an infectious CNS process present? Positive results direct antimicrobial therapy.
Is hypothyroidism causing depressive symptoms? Abnormal TSH supports endocrine cause.
Is substance use contributing? Detects illicit drugs influencing behaviour.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent intervention.
b: Suicidal intent or plan
Psychosis with command hallucinations
Severe agitation risking harm
Rapid deterioration suggesting organic cause

sections.p: Treat underlying causes, then apply psychosocial and pharmacological strategies.
b: Psychotherapy: CBT for anxiety/depression; psychoeducation for adherence
Antidepressants (SSRIs) for mood disorders – chosen for safety, low toxicity
Antipsychotics (typical/atypical) for psychosis – avoid high‑risk EPS in low‑resource settings
Treat infections (e.g., antiretrovirals for HIV, anti‑TB drugs) before psychiatric meds

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, medication side‑effects and social support; relapse prevention plans are essential.
b: Re‑assess severity with PHQ‑9/GAD‑7 every 4‑6 weeks
Monitor adherence, side‑effects, and substance use
Link to community resources, support groups
Delirium (acute, fluctuating consciousness)
Neurological disorders (stroke, epilepsy)
Endocrine disorders (thyroid disease)
Substance‑induced mood changes

sections.p: Lab or clinical findings that may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal CBC in early HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder
Negative drug screen when substances are metabolised quickly
Normal thyroid tests in non‑thyroidal illness syndrome

whenToSeekHelp: Acute psychosis with risk of violence
Rapid cognitive decline suggesting organic brain disease

faq.q: What is the first step in a psychiatric interview?
faq.a: Establish rapport, obtain a concise history and perform a mental status exam.

faq.q: When should I order brain imaging?
faq.a: If there are red‑flag features such as new onset psychosis, focal neurological signs, or rapid cognitive change.

faq.q: Why are SSRIs preferred for depression in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: They have a favorable safety profile, few drug interactions and are widely available.

exam: Describe the biopsychosocial model and its relevance to psychiatric formulation.
List three red‑flag features that require urgent referral in a patient with depressive symptoms.
Explain how you would differentiate major depressive disorder from hypothyroidism‑related depression.
